title: The Transitus (3 October 1226)
hook: Francis dies lying on the bare ground singing Psalm 141

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace prayer, honestly: not his words, but his shape. Your line was francis-shaped.

Evening, at the little church of Saint Mary of the Angels below Assisi. Francis is dying, and he knows it. His brothers crowd around. He's blind or nearly, worn out, and the early lives say he carries wounds in his hands and side. He asks for something strange: take off my habit, and lay me on the bare ground. No bed, no pillow. Just the earth he called sister and mother. Then, the old biographers say, he began to sing. Today, the night Francis died, and the name his brothers gave it.
screen: `EVENING, AT SAINT MARY OF THE ANGELS.` → `LAY ME ON THE BARE GROUND.` → `AND HE BEGAN TO SING.`

segments.voice: Franciscans call that night the Transitus, Latin for a passing over. Not an ending, a crossing. The word echoes the Gospel Francis asked to hear that evening, John chapter thirteen, which opens in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass out of this world to the Father." Francis wanted to die the way his Lord had passed: poor, stripped, among friends. The early lives tell it in pieces. He blesses the brothers around him. In Saint Bonaventure's telling, he says he has done his part; may Christ teach them theirs. Then he sings Psalm one hundred forty-one, as numbered in the Latin Bible the friars prayed: "I cried to the Lord with my voice." Near the end it asks: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name." A dying man asking to be let out, and calling it praise. Earlier, Francis had added a last verse to his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for our Sister Bodily Death, whom no one living can escape. Celano tells that when death came near, Francis greeted it as family: welcome, my sister death. The man who called the sun brother called death sister too. Bonaventure adds a quiet detail: larks, birds of daylight, gathered over the roof at dusk and sang. Sign or lovely story, the brothers remembered it. And if death feels close or wanted for you tonight, please don't carry that alone: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
screen: `TRANSITUS: A PASSING OVER.` · `JOHN 13: HIS HOUR WAS COME.` · `PSALM 141, SUNG ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `DEATH, GREETED AS A SISTER.` · then, large: `BRING MY SOUL OUT OF PRISON.`

segments.voice: Lie flat if you can, on the floor or a bed, arms loose, or lean back and let your body be heavy, and feel the ground holding you up. If you pray, say the line Francis sang, I cried to the Lord with my voice, and rest, then the other: bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name; if not, just notice how it feels to be held, with nothing to do.
The Transitus. Francis's passing over: dying on the bare ground, singing a psalm, greeting death as his sister. Today's word.
Your line: welcome, sister death. For Francis, even the last night was a crossing, met among friends. Go gently tonight.

howItsDone: Franciscans and some parishes keep a Transitus service on the eve of Saint Francis's feast, retelling his death with readings, Psalm 141 and his Canticle of the Creatures, often by candlelight.

chat.says: Why do Franciscans call the night Francis died the Transitus?
options: It means a passing over: they remember his death as a crossing to God, not an ending.
It means the long journey his body made from Assisi to be buried in Rome.
It means a sleep: they hold that he only rested, and woke again days later.
chat.meaning: Transitus is Latin for a passing over; like Jesus passing to the Father in John 13, Francis's death is remembered as a crossing.

notes: Claims rule: the title's date is not repeated in the voice. 'Psalm one hundred forty-one' is the index's own reference (Vulgate numbering); the trapdoor's renumbering note (Hebrew 142) should be confirmed.

Deathbed details paraphrased from Celano and Bonaventure: laid naked on the ground at the Portiuncula; blessing the brothers; 'I have done what is mine; may Christ teach you what is yours' (Bonaventure, LM 14.3); John 13 read aloud; Psalm 141 ('Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi') sung; larks over the roof at dusk (LM 14.6); 'Welcome, my sister death' (Celano, 2 Cel 217). Confirm each attribution.
'He is blind or nearly' and 'carrying wounds in his hands and side' (the stigmata) are stated from the early lives; confirm phrasing.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: John 13:1; Psalm 141:2 and 141:8.
howItsDone: confirm 'some parishes' keep a Transitus service; the date (evening of 3 October) is not stated.
